newsitem.title: UK: Sterling knocked off its perch by Bundesbank.
newsitem.headline: Sterling knocked off its perch by Bundesbank.

text.p: Sterling tumbled near three pfennigs from its earlier perch at a 52-month peak on Wednesday after comments from Germany's Bundesbank cooled speculation Germany favoured a higher dollar.
"The Bundesbank statements have put a cap on mark weakness and sterling has been caught in the crossfire," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ international.
"Before the Bundesbank comments sterling was looking well wanted," said a senior dealer at a UK bank.

Chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber, in an official statement from the central bank, said the Bundesbank continued to believe that the dollar has corrected and did not think it should rise further. He said the Bundesbank continued to support a statement made by the G7 meeting in Berlin last weekend.

The Bundesbank comments, which slapped the dollar lower after it jumped to fresh 34-month peaks of 1.6935 marks, were in response to an MNSI news agency report which said Germany was keen to see a further rise in dollar.
"The opinion expressed in the MNSI report does not exist within the Bundesbank," Koerber said.
Sterling's hefty gains against the mark were also trimmed and the pound dropped near three pfennigs after setting a fresh 52-month peak of 2.7685 marks.
At 1335 GMT, sterling stood at 2.7445/55 marks, well off highs, but still a whisker up from 2.7438/48 in late Europe on Tuesday.

Traders said they were surprised that a dramatic January drop in UK unemployment -- down a seasonally-adjusted 67,800 and more than double the fall expected -- had failed to keep the pound supported at its 52-month peaks. "The figures should have been supportive," said a dealer at a Japanese bank.
Analysts said while the drop in unemployment confirmed tight labour markets and heightened inflationary fears, they did not expect an interest rate rise this side of a general election.

"I think there is a minimal chance for any move in interest rates before the election...I think (Chancellor Kenneth) Clarke has made that very clear," said Brian Hilliard, chief international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.

He said while the unemployment drop was substantial, he remained cautious about the impact of the job seekers allowance and also highlighted disappointing earnings figures, up 4.25 percent in the year to December and above forecasts for an 4.0 percent rise.
"It's a mixed bag. Unemployment is distorted, the average earnings figures disappointing but unit wage costs by contrast are better than expected," he said.
The Bank of England's inflation report on Wednesday also helped to push sterling lower as it seemed to be taking a softer stance against inflation, said traders.
"The bank has softened its tone on inflation," said the trader at the UK bank.
The BoE said it continued to see need for a moderate tightening of monetary policy to ensure the government's 2.5 percent inflation target can be met two years ahead.
"The bank's central projection for inflation two years ahead is close to three percent and rising," it said in its quarterly Inflation Report.
But sterling, the latest darling of currency markets, is poised to regain its upside trend after Wednesday's setback, said analysts.
"The UK fundamentals remain very favourable with the prospect of interest rises still there. Sterling will re-assert itself," Edmonds added.
